items.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
items.summary: vcs, vibecoding
items.content:
Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:

Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:

I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)

I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)

But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.

Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti’s blog post for Cursor .  ↩︎

items.content:
Homeland Security eyes no-bid deal for AI-assisted search of billions of communication records

The system would combine live wiretaps, phone location data, email, and financial records. ICE says only one company can build it.

The Department of Homeland Security plans to give a Nebraska company a no-bid contract for software meant to let federal agents search billions of wiretap, phone, and location records, according to a notice posted Wednesday .

Agents using the system could question an artificial intelligence assistant in plain English. A requirements document attached to the notice calls for a single platform that gathers live wiretaps, call records, email, financial records, and social media data for investigators at Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s criminal investigations branch, Homeland Security Investigations.

ICE said in the notice that Pen-Link Ltd. of Lincoln, Nebraska, is the only company “reasonably available” to do the work because of its capabilities and the “proprietary nature of the services.” The contract calls for one year of work with four one-year options, for a possible five years. The notice gives no dollar amount. Other companies have until 10 a.m. Monday, Oct. 26, to send a one-page response showing they could do the job.

Pen-Link already sells ICE a separate tool called Webloc, which tracks phones using location data collected from mobile apps and digital advertising. ICE pays for access to that data instead of getting it through a court order. The notice does not say whether Webloc data will feed the new system. In March, 72 members of Congress called for an investigation of ICE and other agencies over what they called warrantless purchases of Americans’ location data.

The requirements document describes a system for thousands of agents, with at least 500 using it at the same time in offices across the United States and overseas. The system must store at least 10 terabytes of data, which the document says covers billions of communication records.

The requirements call for live wiretaps and live location “pings” from phones, along with records of who called whom and when. They also list “tower dumps,” which are lists of every phone that connected to a cell tower during a set period and can include many people who are not under investigation. The other data listed includes email, web browsing history, financial records, and social media records from companies such as Google, Facebook, Snapchat, and WhatsApp, along with data copied from seized phones.

The tools described include maps of where phones have been, alerts when a phone enters a marked area, and a phone app that displays live data. The system must also link to a national platform run by the Homeland Security Task Force that flags when two agencies are investigating the same phone number or account.

The document describes an assistant that runs on ICE’s own Microsoft Azure accounts. Agents ask it to summarize, map, and chart the data, and it translates and transcribes recordings. The document says ICE data and agents’ questions may not be used to train outside AI models and that every use of the assistant must be logged. A separate entry in DHS’s public inventory of AI tools describes an ICE project to search and summarize translated wiretap recordings with a large language model. The inventory lists that project as not yet deployed.

The requirements also say the AI assistant must “prevent vendor lock-in,” meaning the agency should not become dependent on one company. The notice does not explain how ICE weighed that goal against its finding that only Pen-Link can do the work.

The notice follows an Aug. 10 request for information in which ICE asked companies about a “Telecommunications Analysis System” with the same features, according to Biometric Update . ICE described that request as market research and said it was not committing to buy anything.

items.title: Surveillance at Scale : How AI training platforms gather personal data from European workers
items.content:
DiPLab is releasing a report on the surveillance of data workers today. Entitled “ Surveillance at Scale : How AI training platforms gather personal data from European workers ” this report is a research project in collaboration with Reversing.works and Intérêt à Agir , funded by the Digital Freedom Fund and the European Artificial Intelligence & Society Fund.

International technology companies collect vast amounts of personal data from European citizens. Public debate and policymaking often focus on data taken from consumers through e-commerce, social media, or streaming platforms. Yet many Europeans also use digital platforms to work and train AI systems.

Online freelance platforms are usually discussed in terms of low pay and insecure “gigs”. Much less attention is given to another resource these platforms extract from workers: their personal data. This report examines the case of Outlier, a key data work platform for artificial intelligence.

Outlier is operated by Scale AI, a company that recruits workers to perform tasks such as evaluating AI-generated responses, creating training data, and improving AI models. This report shows how digital platforms rely on data workers worldwide, including in the EU, to label, check, and organize training data.

These data are harvested online. But Outlier also collects workers’ personal data, financial records, biometric information, and even facial recognition scans. This data is used for surveillance purposes, and probably for further AI training purposes. Our interdisciplinary team analyzes the evidence collected from qualitative interviews, network logs, and guidelines, to provide evidence of a large-scale data collection process, through hidden trackers.

We also provide a legal analysis in terms of likely European law (GDPR) data protection violations : the AI WORLd project reveals how the EU has become a periphery for data extractivism in the production process of AI models. Ethical AI requires the ethical treatment of the modern-day factory workers whose work makes it possible. Beyond the economic exploitation data workers through inadequate compensation, this report reveals the extraction of personal data for purposes ranging from covert AI training to potential military applications. These practices raise serious concerns about social justice, labor law, and European data security.

items.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
items.content:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

items.title: Introducing Firefox Enterprise
items.summary: browsers, release, web
items.content:
Institutions are recalculating who controls the technology they rely on. Mozilla has an independent option to offer.

For years, organizations consolidated technology around a small number of providers to make things simpler. Fewer systems. Tighter integrations. More economies of scale. But that consolidation went well beyond technology. It consolidated dependency, too. The resulting risks have been debated, studied, and challenged along the way, but concentration continued. More work, data and critical infrastructure kept moving to the same few providers, while credible alternatives narrowed.

The deeper that dependency runs, the harder and more costly it becomes to change course. When something fails, changes or falls outside an institution’s control, that dependency becomes a risk for CIOs and CISOs to manage.

Nowhere are these stakes more visible than in Europe. Now institutions are re-assessing. Governments are pushing for greater digital autonomy, while regulated industries face growing pressure to find and manage their dependencies.

There’s a name for much of this debate about technological control: “sovereignty.”

What digital sovereignty means in practice varies. Across Europe, governments are investing in the security and resilience of critical IT infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies and putting technological autonomy higher on national agendas. Different approaches, same underlying concern. Strip away the regional policy definitions and industry distinctions and a pretty practical, universal question emerges: how much technological dependency should we risk?

And a very specific, very important layer has been largely missing from that conversation: the browser.

The browser. Applications run there. Employees authenticate in it. Sensitive data transits through it. Files are uploaded and downloaded and AI tools are increasingly used through it. That raises the same questions of dependency and control: whose browser technology are you relying on, and who controls the infrastructure used to manage it?

Firefox Enterprise is built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements. It pairs the Firefox browser, built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, with a management console organizations can run on their own infrastructure. From that console, IT teams can centrally manage browser policy and access, govern how data moves through the browser and set controls around AI use.

IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience.

“If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” said Anthony Enzor-DeMeo, CEO of Mozilla. “We built Firefox differently. And we’re bringing its independent architecture to institutions that are ready to rethink their dependencies and risk.”

We’re starting with the browser because we see it as a key, but under-governed, layer. Firefox Enterprise gives institutions more control over the browser and the infrastructure managing it.

And because Firefox runs on Gecko, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple, institutions have another path towards reducing dependence on a single architecture.

Finally, Firefox Enterprise is built to live alongside the systems that IT operations already use. Keep your identity provider. Keep your SIEM. Keep your MDM. Just add a browser whose management infrastructure you operate, so you decide where data lives and have greater visibility into how it moves.

For us, supporting the goal of technological sovereignty comes down to four things: More control. More transparency. More choice. More resilience.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
items.content:
Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.

But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...

Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over : the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.

Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales . But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!

Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.

Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.

There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.

Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.

Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:

In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.

Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.

Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.

Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller , if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.

The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.

It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit , California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.

Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.

For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales . For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.

At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon,…

items.title: What I Self-Host
items.summary: devops
items.content:
I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV , then XBMC (later known as Kodi).

Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.

So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin . Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.

With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service.

I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There’s no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.

Related, I don’t do Docker anymore. It’s not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I’m already using systemd, and at this point Podman’s integration with systemd is excellent.

Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.

items.title: Other AI Companies Should Be Very Afraid of What Just Happened to Character.AI, According to Its Own Bankruptcy Documents: Be afraid.
items.content:
So far, the top AI companies have been sustained by constant injections of massive investment. But what happens when the funds stop coming in and they’re expected to survive on their own revenue?

The fate of Character.AI, the controversial AI companion platform, may come to stand as a warning.

On Tuesday, Character.AI filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy , marking the beginning of an ignominious end for a once-buzzy startup valued at a billion dollars. Its bankruptcy filings, which were picked through by 404 Media , encapsulate the critiques of the AI industry’s model. It gained a huge user base with a highly engaging product, but racked up exorbitant compute bills while failing to monetize all the time people were spending talking to its chatbots. All the while, it became mired in lawsuits alleging that its products harmed its teenage users or even encouraged their suicides.

In the documentation, the company is candid about its failings. CEO Colin Adams sums it up by saying its “impressive technology is expensive to operate,” and that it’s consistently “struggled with profitability and its operational expenditure has been high.”

In numbers, that looked like $56.1 million spent on compute costs between January and August 2026, while spending an additional $19.7 million on employee salaries during the same period.

Its revenue remained dismal, picking up from $2.8 million in December 2025 to $5.3 million for the month of August — while still running at an operating loss of $8 to 9 million per month.

Desperate to stop the bleeding, the company resorted to “enshittifying” its product, as 404 puts it. It started shoving more ads, enforcing tighter usage limits, and foisting cheaper “lobotomized” models on its users.

The company also “reduced its employee headcount,” Adams wrote. “In mid-2025, Character launched in-app advertising,” and “in early 2026, Character also introduced in-app purchases.”

For a startup that once promised it would bring “personalized superintelligence” to everyone on Earth, its business model, and the experience of using its app, began to sound indistinguishable from a sleazy mobile game.

Attracting millions of users, clearly, doesn’t guarantee long term success. More users meant more compute costs, and the nature of how users interacted with the chatbots — as companions — meant they were being put through hours-long, extensive conversations. It became a big bill to foot.

The same could be said for most major AI products. Many people have close relationships with ChatGPT or Claude. Power users leverage them to churn out mountains of code, often running multiple instances at the same time to handle different tasks. In many cases, these AI providers have already switched up their pricing schemes to direct usage-based billing to respond to the rising compute costs. OpenAI, meanwhile, began showing ads in ChatGPT to free and low paid tier users this year. And like Character.AI, it’s also been hit with multiple lawsuits alleging its chatbot drove users to suicide .

For now, the leading AI companies can stay afloat by attracting huge investment (OpenAI and Anthropic), or subsidizing their AI operations with their traditional revenue streams (Google and Meta). But eventually there’ll come a time when the training wheels come off — and at that point, Character.AI’s demise may start to feel like a cautionary tale.

items.title: Introducing the Accessible Components Library
items.content:
We've open-sourced our Accessible Components Library , and, as you might expect, this includes the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. But, we thought, "Why stop there?" So, we've also published our documentation, including the accessibility requirements, test scenarios, and even the working automated tests which validate each one.

Here's what we've released, how it works, and why automated tests are worth the effort. One caveat: these components are opinionated and built for our needs. Feel free to reuse or adapt them, but test them in your product before relying on them. They're not a production-ready design system.

As part of our efforts to provide useful resources to the accessibility community, we've released version 1.0.0, which includes eight components. We will be releasing more in the future, but for now you can check out:

Each component ships with working examples, the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript behind it, and documentation which explains:

The accessibility requirements are the part which we think separates what we're doing from other component libraries. For every component, we've documented the applicable success criteria from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 , at levels A, AA, and AAA. We've also added our own recommendations for things WCAG doesn't cover, such as usability when using high contrast themes.

Because WCAG can be challenging to navigate, we've grouped the requirements into ten themes, including:

This should make it easier to quickly understand how a component meets the needs of the people who use it.

Because there's always some technical jargon and caveats, we've also published our:

Documenting requirements is useful, but a document can't tell you whether a component actually meets them all. So, we converted each requirement into a test scenario using Gherkin syntax, and we wrote working Cucumber tests which validate them.

Gherkin is great because it describes complicated automated tests in plain language, using Given , When , and Then to describe each step. This makes it easier for non-developers to understand what the test is doing, and even help write tests. We've written about Gherkin before, and why it helps to annotate designs using common language .

Each of our Gherkin scenarios includes the following:

For example, here's our scenario for 1.4.10 Reflow on the breadcrumbs component:

This matters because you don't need to be able to read all the complex JavaScript code to understand what the test is doing. A designer, a tester, a product manager and a developer can all read the same scenario, and all agree on what it means to pass or fail. And, even if you don't use JavaScript on your project, because Cucumber is available in most mainstream programming languages, you can still use the Gherkin feature files and write your own tests to validate them.

All of our test scenarios are written from a collection of shared steps, which was a lot of work at the beginning, because we had to write the underlying code to validate each one. But, each step is reusable, so scaling is easy.

We've published a full list of our test steps which work out of the box. This list is generated from the actual step definitions we use in the repository, so it's kept in sync automatically. This means any time we add a new one, you'll also get it for free.

Behind each test step is JavaScript code that controls a real browser using Playwright . The tests load the sample from a URL, and then interact with it the same way a real person would, by clicking things or focusing them using a keyboard. Then, they pull information from the browser, like the states and properties of the elements, and verify whether the things that were supposed to happen actually happened.

items.title: Do dentists know what they're doing?
items.content:
Do dentists actually know what they’re doing?

I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both because my teeth are straight and even. Good thing, because I’m in high school and braces would dissolve what small nuggets of game I have.

‘Well!’ declares the dentist as he emerges from my mouth. He pulls off his glove and I close my jaw. There’s a pop that could have come from either.

‘The thing is that the two halves of your face didn’t grow at the same rate. Here, take a look.’ He holds up a mirror and I see my disfiguration for the first time. The right side of my jaw is a little crooked. My nose on that side is angled, my eyelid is a slightly different shape.

I am shocked and embarrassed. I touch my face. I had no idea.

‘No, but your bite is a bit off. Fractions of a millimeter here and there.’ His own teeth strobe out from between his lips as he talks. They rival the overhead lamp for xenon brilliance, accentuated by his deeply tanned skin.

‘You’ll want to get it corrected or you could end up wearing your teeth down. I can do it today if you’re up for it?’

‘Oh it will make that better actually. Your jaw will slot right into place after this. No more sliding around to find the right bite.’

‘If you were my son, I would say the same thing.’

Tooth reshaping was a euphemism. Voluntary torture would have been more accurate. My teeth fit together better alright. But they are shorter now, and that makes the impingement of my jaw into the right socket worse.

Fucking guy. Never going there again. That hygienist was pretty though…mom-pretty because she was like 28, but still.

I wish I had never done it. But hey, at least I didn’t have to get braces.

I’m 20, in Florida. My face is still warm from the radiation bath the ancient x-ray machine gave me. It is a tall, forbidding machine that would have at least a dozen skulls painted on its nose cone if it was a fighter plane. The office is a couple rooms in an office building basement. The hygienist is out for another back surgery and the front desk lady is sick. So the sweaty old dentist is doing it all himself today.

‘Well no cavities,’ he murmurs, looking at the pictures. The good news momentarily lifts the weary folds at the edge of his mouth but the smile does not reach his sad eyes.

‘Great,’ I say. I expected no less. I am 20 after all, and I will live forever.

‘But looks like you’ve started to grind your teeth. And you say the jaw hurts?’

‘Grind my teeth? I don’t think so.’ I run my tongue along the inside of my teeth.

‘Well, it happens when you’re asleep so you don’t notice.’

‘Well, I can make you a splint. That’ll help both issues. It’s like a retainer that your front teeth rest on. It allows them to glide a few millimeters above the others so you don’t grind. And it will probably allow your jaw to relax.’

‘Not really once you get used to it. I just made one for my daughter.’

I’m 22, and living in Utah. The splint was great but I’ve lost it and I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. I looked up the top-rated dentist on Google and now I’m walking into my appointment.

I open the door and squint into the shining plasticky sleekness. ‘Hello and welcome!’ beams a beautiful girl with flowing blonde hair and red lips. She sits in a Herman Miller chair behind a white marble countertop. The lights are bright and fancy green wallpaper accents one wall. The office air is chilly, fancy chilly, the kind of chilly that says ‘we don’t care how much electricity costs, as long as you’re comfortable .’

The hygienist that does my cleaning is also beautiful, about my age. Ring on though…my sister was a hygienist for a while and wore a fake ring to keep the men at bay. 22 and married? This is Utah, so probably legit.

When did they start cutting scrubs to make them sexy?

Another girl takes my x-rays on a new machine the size of a small ottoman. She is also beautiful and also…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
items.content:
Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it.

This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded.

Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs.

Raising the red flag are researchers at White Circle, a public benefit corporation backed by senior leaders and researchers from Anthropic, DeepMind, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It was founded after CEO Denis Shilov posted one of the most famous universal jailbreaks of leading models in October 2024. Bent on breaking models to conduct thorough safety testing, White Circle helps companies detect and deter threats when implementing advanced AI systems that may not always behave as expected.

Testing how well text-to-image models block banned content categories is a key research direction for White Circle, and Shilov thinks their latest findings are “horrifying” enough to share with the public.

In a little-noticed preprint published last month, White Circle researchers exposed flaws in the guardrails of DALL·E 3, Google’s Nano Banana 2, and GPT-Image-2. In a press release, they explained that “using just off-the-shelf tools, available online for anyone to download, and by sending API calls, White Circle was able to use the novel attack method to bypass the safety filters.” In the best case, on DALL·E 3, about 13 percent of the attack prompts produced images that human reviewers confirmed as explicit. The rate was under 10 percent for Nano Banana 2 and about 3 percent for GPT-Image-2.

“Critically, none of these requests required custom-built or frontier AI models,” White Circle warned.

Researchers reviewed the outputs to verify the bypass rate, which White Circle noted is “the highest of any method tested under the same standard.” The key takeaway, they suggested, is that, “at a time when AI safety has never been under more scrutiny, the defenses leading labs have built are far weaker than they acknowledge.”

By publishing research like this, White Circle is positioning itself as an external evaluator of frontier labs, and it plans to open-source the entire attack pipeline so model makers can understand the true scale of the vulnerability and build stronger protections. Although the company has not widely promoted the research yet, it will share it at a prominent AI conference this November, NeurIPS 2026, which may increase scrutiny on Google and OpenAI later this fall.

White Circle has shared its findings with some frontier AI labs through “mutual contacts,” Shilov told Ars, but neither Google nor OpenAI responded to Ars’ request to comment directly on vulnerabilities found in their models.

Meanwhile, OpenAI and Google have released new models—ChatGPT Images 2.5 and Nano Banana 2.1—and White Circle told Ars that prompt safety testing using the same method showed “both are significantly more breakable than their previous versions.”

Neither company responded after Ars shared these new findings.

White Circle’s attack method can break down frontier defenses in categories, like explicit content, that seem easy to spot, which doesn’t bode well for more serious defense systems currently being updated to block other unwanted AI behavior, like hacking, Shilov told Ars.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
items.content:
EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post.

The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process.

TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “ committed to protecting traveler privacy ,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case.

The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.”

TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed.

We hope the TSA will fix these issues. The OIG summary states:

We issued one finding and three recommendations to strengthen controls, improve oversight, and ensure transparency and the proper handling of passenger data. TSA concurred with all three recommendations. Two recommendations are open and resolved, and one remains open and unresolved.

Why EFF Opposes the Government’s Use of Facial Recognition Technology

EFF has a long history of opposing governmental use of facial recognition technology. As the OIG’s audit underscores, this technology presents privacy risks associated with unsecured data, unauthorized access, and data breaches. The government’s use of this technology also creates a mass surveillance system and facilitates the creation of warrantless biometric records for unconsenting parties.

The biometric data captured by this technology is not without errors. There have been multiple instances of law enforcement agencies using facial recognition technology to misidentify and arrest innocent individuals.

Reminder: Opting Out of TSA Photos Is Possible

Given that facial recognition technology is prone to mistakes, combined with the OIG’s audit revealing significant privacy weaknesses, it is imperative that travelers remember that opting out is possible. TSA’s own website emphasizes that travelers who wish to decline to have their photo taken for facial comparison can do so without any delay, disruption, or recourse.

Considering the data protection weaknesses exposed by the OIG’s audit, EFF will continue to oppose this governmental system of mass surveillance and spread awareness to ensure that no one is forced to relinquish their biometric data without consent.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Dutch tax authorities cancel Microsoft 365 cloud rollout - and turn toward open source - ZDNET

ED OUDENAARDEN / Contributor/ AFP via Getty Images

The Netherlands stopped a government agency’s shift to Microsoft 365.

The drive toward an open-source, digital sovereignty approach continues.

What the Netherlands will move to next is quite vague.

The Netherlands’ Tax and Customs Administration has abandoned its planned Microsoft 365 public-cloud rollout .

Why? The reasons were clear at the Open Source Summit Europe conference, where the Linux Foundation (LF) released the 2026 State of Open Source in Europe . In it, the nonprofit, pro-open-source organization revealed that 94% of European Union (EU) organizations say digital sovereignty is important, with 61% considering it very important. As Thierry Carrez, the Linux Foundation Europe GM, said in his keynote, “Europe has clearly heard the message on digital sovereignty.”

Why the future of Linux is rolling – thanks to AI

Windows update patches a whopping 1,400 security bugs –  including 2 zero days

It’s not just the Dutch tax collectors, though. The Netherlands is also exploring switching from Windows and proprietary software to Linux and open-source programs across the board . That follows the Swiss military and other agencies announcing they were moving to Linux and openDesk , a German open-source office suite. Before that, European governments shifting to Linux included Austria , France , Germany , and Ireland .

Also: Windows October update patches a whopping 1,400 security bugs –  including 2 zero days

Indeed, according to the LF Europe report, 94% of organizations care about AI as much as they do about digital sovereignty. We all know how businesses are moving to AI as fast as they can. Outside the States, the move to digital sovereignty is garnering just as much support.

The Netherlands had planned to switch to Microsoft 365 in 2025. The idea then was to complete the rollout by the end of 2026. About 5,000 employees had already migrated when the Dutch Advisory Council on ICT Assessment recommended reversing the public-cloud rollout in June. The government paused the plan in July; the latest announcement replaces that rollout with an on-premises/open-source approach.

The Tax and Customs Administration isn’t replacing all of Microsoft Office with a single open-source suite, at least not yet. Instead, the government will keep the existing Microsoft software for now.

Later in 2027 and 2028, European open-source solutions for personal storage and collaboration will follow. This allows us to work toward a sustainable and more autonomous solution for these functionalities.”

items.title: Symfony UX 3.6 released
items.content:
Symfony UX 3.6 is out, with more than 100 pull requests merged since 3.5.1. It

adds three experimental packages, UX Inspector, UX Image and UX Router, aligns

the Shadcn kit of the UX Toolkit with the Nova style, and runs every Toolkit

recipe in a real browser, which led to about thirty fixes in the kits.

Stimulus controllers, LiveComponents and Turbo frames are spread

across the DOM as data-* attributes, and the browser devtools give you no

overview of them. UX Inspector is a devtools panel for Symfony UX that outlines

every controller, component and frame of the page.

Pick one on the page to jump to its details, which update while the

application runs. Open the panel with the pull tab on the right edge of the

screen, or type u then x outside an editable field.

Stimulus : values and their defaults, targets, CSS classes, actions and

outlets, and whether the controller is connected;

LiveComponent : props and parent props, models and their modifiers,

actions and their arguments, event listeners, loading and polling;

Turbo : the source URL, loading strategy and state of each frame, nested

The activity log lists events in the order they fire: LiveComponent renders,

Turbo fetches with their status and duration, controller events. This first

version only reads the page, and only runs in debug mode.

The Flex recipe, which registers the bundle in dev and connects your

Stimulus application to it, is still in review ( symfony/recipes#1586 ). The

guided demos on the UX website show the Inspector at work.

A responsive image needs several variants of the same file, a srcset that

lists them and a sizes attribute that matches the layout. UX Image

generates all three, but it never decodes, resizes or encodes an image itself:

every variant is a URL, and an image CDN does the work.

Nothing is transformed by default. Every variant comes from an external CDN,

through a bridge you install, and switching CDNs never touches a template. Four

bridges ship with this release, each in its own package: Cloudflare ,

items.title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
items.content:
Americans’ Social Activity Has Steeply Declined in the Past 30 Years

In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”

Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points , from 63% to 38%.

But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.

In a new survey , Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.

This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026 .

The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).

A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).

Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.

One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.

Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.

The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.

There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.

This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.

items.title: Yandex outage: data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move
items.content:
Following reported strikes on Yandex data centers, claims circulated on the Internet that Russian bot farms and influence operations had been knocked offline. HTTP traffic charts showed steep drops, fueling speculation that the infrastructure damage had stopped these malicious actors. However, aggregate traffic metrics can easily mislead. There are two autonomous system numbers ( ASNs ) associated with Yandex: AS13238 is used by Yandex’s search engine, while AS200350 runs its cloud services.

Using Cloudflare Radar and Bot Management data, we analyzed how these two ASNs were affected — and while both saw drops in traffic, they saw differing impact.

Yandex Search (AS13238) :  The drop in traffic consisted almost entirely of verified search crawlers indexing web pages, images, and site resources.

Yandex.Cloud (AS200350): There was a decline in malicious activities like vulnerability scanning and probing, but high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.

While malicious traffic may originate from a particular provider, it does not necessarily tell us who is responsible for the traffic. Understanding why the strikes had little lasting effect on malicious traffic requires analyzing request behavior, rather than just overall traffic patterns.

What happened: the effect of the strikes and pre-event baseline

Between October 7 and 11, reported Ukrainian drone strikes hit three Yandex facilities in Russia, progressively knocking data centers and network capacity offline. As seen on Cloudflare Radar , this culminated in a near-total collapse of the Yandex network on October 11 when traffic plummeted to 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350). Despite a brief partial recovery, both networks remained disrupted through October 13, settling at 86-90% below normal baselines. (As of October 14 at 18:00 UTC, traffic is at 85% of normal.)

A drop in overall HTTP traffic only confirms that the network went down. It does not reveal whether malicious or evasive bots were disrupted. Looking at the pre-event automation baseline, we can see that before the strikes, automated requests accounted for 36.1% of all HTTP traffic observed globally  across Cloudflare's network, and 35.8% of traffic from Russian IP addresses .

The outage had different effects on automated activity on the two affected ASNs because they served different roles.

Yandex Search ASN (AS13238)  is used for search index crawling. Cloudflare classified 99.5% of its requests as automated, and 93.6% of its bot requests as Verified . Our analysis showed that traffic from this ASN indexed pages, rendered pages, and rendered images, which is consistent behavior for a search crawler. The Yandex Search ASN supplied about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.05% of the global total.

Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350)  is a cloud-hosting network and carries a very different mix of automation. Approximately 95.0% of its scored requests were bots, but none of its observed bot requests were verified by Cloudflare. Yandex.Cloud’s bots looked more like software apps: nearly two-thirds of their requests sent data to websites, some identified themselves as JavaScript, Python, or Go programs, and a larger share went to software companies than Yandex’s search bots. The Yandex.Cloud ASN supplied about 2% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.01% of the global total.

Impact of the event on overall bot traffic

"Bot traffic" refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms. As Yandex’s networks lost capacity, their bot requests fell too. That was expected: nearly all traffic from Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud was automated. While we saw the obvious drop in total traffic, we did not see any evidence linking a global disruption in malicious traffic to the drop in traffic from Yandex.

items.title: Designing for people who are colour blind
items.content:
Colour blindness can get overlooked in accessible design, but it can have a significant impact on how people access the web, making it harder to notice important information, distinguish interactive elements, or understand data that relies on colour alone.

Colour blindness, also called colour vision deficiency (CVD), is a condition where a person cannot see the full spectrum of colours. This results in people having trouble telling specific colours apart, especially when those colours are placed next to each other or viewed in low light.

Most people who are colour blind are born with it, although ageing, some medications, and conditions like diabetes can also cause it. It's also more common in men , affecting about one in 12 men and one in 200 women.

Red-green is the most common colour deficiency and can range from difficulty discerning particular shades to recognising only three or four colours.

The most common forms are protanopia and deuteranopia:

With both types, red and green can look like shades of brown or yellow, and blue and purple can look the same.

As is often the case with inclusive design, designing for specific people benefits many more people.

Designing for people who are colour blind often aligns closely with best practices for internationalisation and cross-cultural design. Colours carry different meanings across cultures, so by avoiding reliance on colour alone or the cultural meanings we assign to colours, we can create content that works well globally.

Finally, designs that don’t rely solely on colour are easier to interpret in bright sunlight or on screens with glare. For example, charts that use both patterns and colour to differentiate data remain readable even when colours wash out under poor lighting.

Inclusive design goes beyond the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) . Designing for people who are colour blind is a shared responsibility between editors, copywriters, designers, and developers.

WCAG Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.1, use of colour , states that colour should never be the only way information is conveyed. In other words, pair colour with something else that communicates the same information, such as an icon, a pattern, or a text label.

If you’re using icons and colours together to show different states, make sure the icons are distinct enough to be useful. A good example of this is Slack’s status indicators. Both the “active” and “away” states are represented by circles, but Slack combines multiple cues. The active state is a filled circle (green, if you can perceive it), while the away state uses an outlined circle with an empty centre. This change in both colour and shape clearly communicates a difference, even for people who can’t rely on colour perception.

Away and active state with protanopia filter:

WCAG also covers colour contrast requirements both for text and non-text elements. In practice, this means ensuring there’s enough visual contrast between text and background colours, adjacent interface elements, and different states such as active and inactive buttons.

While we strongly discourage tricky colour combinations that are known to cause issues for people with certain types of colour blindness, ensuring sufficient contrast can at least make those combinations more perceivable, even if they’re not ideal. Something that may be less known is that the colour contrast algorithm works across colour blindness types. So if it is 4.5:1 for standard vision it's also 4.5:1 for people who are colour blind.

All of that said, the best approach is to go a step further and choose colour combinations thoughtfully.

Colour contrast aside, there are certain colour combinations that should just be avoided when designing for everyone but in particular people with protanopia and deuteranopia.

For someone with protanopia or deuteranopia, purple and blue can appear very similar, making them difficult to distinguish.

items.title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?
items.content:
Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?

read (correction: skimmed) a 25,000-word post by rationalist blogger Scott

Alexander. My piece, which cited (but does not focus on) his, ended up being a

cool 2,700 words. I don't think it would benefit from being longer, and it was

the result of me cutting around 70% of the text I initially wrote.

Rationalist bloggers do not generally appear to have this impulse. Eliezer Yudkowsky's

contains some good ideas, is painfully long and extremely tedious. These

bloggers tend to spend their time on precisely the wrong things, i.e.

adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating

the one or two assumptions they make at the start or

broadening their philosophical background beyond the

collection of texts popular within their subculture.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.
